lead: Thursday's readings are about not losing heart. In the NRSV both use the same words: Hebrews tells us to consider Jesus “so that you may not grow weary or lose heart” (12:3), and Luke introduces the parable of the widow with “their need to pray always and not to lose heart” (18:1). One reading points to the runners who have finished before us and to Jesus at the finish; the other to a woman who would not stop asking.

set: Chapter 11 has just listed the heroes of faith, from Abel to the prophets and martyrs, and ended by saying that they “did not receive what was promised” (11:39). Now the writer draws the conclusion with “Therefore”. The picture is a stadium: the runners on the track, the crowd around them, the finishing line ahead.
str: v. 1: surrounded by witnesses, lay aside every weight and run.
v. 2: look to Jesus, who endured the Cross and is now seated at God's right hand.
v. 3: consider him, so as not to grow weary.
kw: A great crowd. They are witnesses first because they bore witness to God by their lives; the picture of spectators watching a race is also present.
A contest, a struggle; the word from which “agony” comes. The Christian life is pictured as an athletic contest that needs endurance.
Jesus is the one who goes ahead and opens the way, and the one who brings faith to its goal. He has run the whole course himself.
vv: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses,
The saints are not distant figures but companions who have finished their race and now encourage ours.
who for the sake of the joy that was set before him endured the cross, disregarding its shame,

The small Greek word anti can mean “for the sake of” or “instead of”. The NRSV takes the first: he endured for the joy ahead. Others read it as: he set aside the joy that was his and chose the Cross, and the Malayalam Bible follows this reading. Both are true of Christ (Philippians 2:6–8).
Consider him who endured such hostility against himself from sinners,
The cure for weariness is not to look at ourselves but at him.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of the witnesses of faith: we must turn to them, and above all to Jesus, “the pioneer and perfecter of our faith” (CCC 165). It also teaches that the witnesses who have gone before us into the Kingdom, especially those the Church recognizes as saints, share in the living tradition of prayer and pray for us (CCC 2683).

r.h: Pray always and do not lose heart
set: The parable follows Jesus' teaching on the coming of the Son of Man (17:20–37). Luke tells us its meaning before he tells the story. In Israel a widow was the classic example of a person without protection, and the Law commanded special care for widows (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18). Judges were to judge fairly and take no bribes (Deuteronomy 16:18–20). This judge, Jesus says, neither feared God nor had respect for people (18:2).
str: v. 1: the purpose of the parable.
vv. 2–5: the judge and the widow.
vv. 6–8a: the lesson: how much more will God do justice.
kw: To grow weary, to give up. Paul uses the same verb when he says, “we do not lose heart” (2 Corinthians 4:16).
Give a just verdict for me, vindicate me. She is not asking for revenge but for her rights.
Literally “strike under the eye”, a boxing term (Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 9:27). The judge says, half in jest, that she will end up giving him a black eye.
vv: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
The parable is not about wearing God down. It is about our need: we stop praying before God stops listening.
And will not God grant justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night?
The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. If even this judge gives in, how much more will God, who is just and who loves his chosen ones.
And yet, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?”
The question turns back on the hearer. God's faithfulness is not in doubt; ours is.
ch: The Catechism names this as one of the three chief parables on prayer in Luke, centred on one quality of prayer: we must pray always, without ceasing, with the patience of faith (CCC 2613). The Syriac Churches have always loved praying through the day; in our tradition the Shehimo, the prayer of the hours, is one way of answering this command to pray always.

study: What “weight” do I need to lay aside so that I can run more lightly toward Christ?
For what intention have I stopped praying because the answer seemed slow? Can I take it up again this week?
